If we run it on (a2,a1)(a_2,a_1)(a2​,a1​) instead, do we get q2,q1q_2,q_1q2​,q1​? If true, explain briefly; if not, give a simple counterexample. (Hint: use the geometric picture.)
🔍Where does this come from?why the new vector is perpendicular to the old ones

Take the second step, q~2=a2−(q1⊤a2) q1\tilde q_2=a_2-(q_1^\top a_2)\,q_1q~​2​=a2​−(q1⊤​a2​)q1​, and compute its inner product with q1q_1q1​:
q1⊤q~2=q1⊤a2−(q1⊤a2) q1⊤q1⏟= 1=q1⊤a2−q1⊤a2=0.q_1^\top\tilde q_2=q_1^\top a_2-(q_1^\top a_2)\,\underbrace{q_1^\top q_1}_{=\,1}=q_1^\top a_2-q_1^\top a_2=0 .q1⊤​q~​2​=q1⊤​a2​−(q1⊤​a2​)=1q1⊤​q1​​​=q1⊤​a2​−q1⊤​a2​=0.
So q~2⊥q1\tilde q_2\perp q_1q~​2​⊥q1​. The same calculation works at every step: when we take the inner product of q~i\tilde q_iq~​i​ with an earlier qjq_jqj​, the subtraction removes exactly qj⊤aiq_j^\top a_iqj⊤​ai​, and all the other subtracted terms vanish because qj⊤qk=0q_j^\top q_k=0qj⊤​qk​=0 for k≠jk\neq jk=j.

Why q~i=0\tilde q_i=\mathbf 0q~​i​=0 means dependence. If nothing is left after removing all the earlier directions, then aia_iai​ was made entirely of earlier directions — it is a combination of the previous vectors.

Remember

Gram–Schmidt means "subtract the projections onto what you already have, then normalise"; a zero remainder q~i=0\tilde q_i=\mathbf 0q~​i​=0 means that aia_iai​ was dependent on the earlier vectors.

#17. Vector spaces, subspaces and dimension

🧩Background you needwhat 'closed' means

A set is closed under an operation if doing that operation to members of the set always gives another member.

  • The even numbers are closed under addition: even +++ even is even.
  • The odd numbers are not: 3+5=83+5=83+5=8 is even.

A subspace must be closed under addition and under multiplication by any scalar, and must contain 0\mathbf 00. The quick test is: "if I add two of its members, or stretch one by any number (including 000 and negative numbers), do I stay inside?"

Example. The line y=2xy=2xy=2x through the origin: (1,2)+(3,6)=(4,8)(1,2)+(3,6)=(4,8)(1,2)+(3,6)=(4,8) is still on it, and −5⋅(1,2)=(−5,−10)-5\cdot(1,2)=(-5,-10)−5⋅(1,2)=(−5,−10) is still on it. Non-example. The line y=2x+1y=2x+1y=2x+1: multiplying the point (0,1)(0,1)(0,1) by 000 gives (0,0)(0,0)(0,0), which is not on the line.

Definition: Vector space

A vector space is a set VVV equipped with addition and multiplication by scalars such that, for all u,v,w∈Vu,v,w\in Vu,v,w∈V and all a,b∈Ra,b\in\mathbb{R}a,b∈R:

  1. u+v∈Vu+v\in Vu+v∈V (closure under addition);
  2. u+v=v+uu+v=v+uu+v=v+u;
  3. (u+v)+w=u+(v+w)(u+v)+w=u+(v+w)(u+v)+w=u+(v+w);
  4. there is a zero vector 0∈V\mathbf 0\in V0∈V with v+0=vv+\mathbf 0=vv+0=v;
  5. every uuu has an inverse −u∈V-u\in V−u∈V with u+(−u)=0u+(-u)=\mathbf 0u+(−u)=0;
  6. au∈Vau\in Vau∈V (closure under scalar multiplication);
  7. a(u+v)=au+ava(u+v)=au+ava(u+v)=au+av;
  8. (a+b)u=au+bu(a+b)u=au+bu(a+b)u=au+bu;
  9. (ab)u=a(bu)(ab)u=a(bu)(ab)u=a(bu);
  10. 1u=u1u=u1u=u.

The main example is Rn\mathbb{R}^nRn. Others listed in the outline include the polynomials of degree at most ddd and spaces of functions: any objects for which these ten rules hold.

Worked example: A set that is not a vector space: physical traffic states

Queue lengths are never negative, so physical traffic states lie in R≥04\mathbb{R}^4_{\ge 0}R≥04​. This set is not a vector space, because multiplying a state by −1-1−1 leaves it. The ambient mathematical space remains R4\mathbb{R}^4R4; the physics merely selects a subset of it.

Definition: Subspace

Let VVV be a vector space and W⊆VW\subseteq VW⊆V. If WWW is itself a vector space under the same operations, it is a subspace. In practice, WWW is a subspace exactly when:

  1. 0∈W\mathbf 0\in W0∈W (non-emptiness);
  2. u,v∈Wu,v\in Wu,v∈W implies u+v∈Wu+v\in Wu+v∈W (closure under addition);
  3. a∈Ra\in\mathbb{R}a∈R and u∈Wu\in Wu∈W imply au∈Wau\in Wau∈W (closure under scalar multiplication).

Compactly: αu+βv∈W\alpha u+\beta v\in Wαu+βv∈W for all u,v∈Wu,v\in Wu,v∈W and all α,β∈R\alpha,\beta\in\mathbb{R}α,β∈R.

Every vector space VVV has at least two subspaces: VVV itself and the zero subspace {0}\{\mathbf 0\}{0}.

Slide examples — subspace or not?

Set Subspace? Reason
a line through the origin yes sums and multiples stay on the line
a plane through the origin in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 yes the same closure argument
a line not through the origin no it does not contain 0\mathbf 00 (multiply any point by 000)
the first quadrant no multiplying a point by −1-1−1 leaves it
a line together with a plane no, in general a point of the line plus a point of the plane can leave the union, unless the line lies in the plane

A span is always a subspace. A combination of combinations of v1,…,vkv_1,\dots,v_kv1​,…,vk​ is again a combination of them (PSet 1, Problem 6), and 0=∑i0⋅vi\mathbf 0=\sum_i 0\cdot v_i0=∑i​0⋅vi​ is in the span.

📄 Original questionPSet 1 · Problem 6 ↗tap to show

Suppose each of b1,b2b_1,b_2b1​,b2​ is a linear combination of a1,a2a_1,a_2a1​,a2​, and ccc is a linear combination of b1,b2b_1,b_2b1​,b2​. Show that ccc must then be a linear combination of a1,a2a_1,a_2a1​,a2​.

Definition: Dimension

The dimension of VVV, written dim⁡(V)\dim(V)dim(V), is the number of vectors in any basis of VVV; every basis has the same number. A line through the origin in R4\mathbb{R}^4R4 has dimension 111, a plane through the origin in R3\mathbb{R}^3R3 has dimension 222, dim⁡Rn=n\dim\mathbb{R}^n=ndimRn=n, and dim⁡{0}=0\dim\{\mathbf 0\}=0dim{0}=0. The subspace S=span⁡{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}⊂R3S=\operatorname{span}\{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)\}\subset\mathbb{R}^3S=span{(1,0,1),(0,1,1)}⊂R3 has dim⁡S=2\dim S=2dimS=2, even though its vectors have three entries.

The valid subspace properties in 2024 Mid MCQ 1 are non-emptiness, closure under addition and closure under scalar multiplication — not "dimension at least 2".

📄 Original question2024 Mid Part I · MCQ 1 ↗tap to show
  • 2024 MCQ 1. Which of the following are valid subspace properties? (a) non-emptiness (b) closure under vector addition (c) dimension must be ≥2\ge2≥2 (d) closure under scalar multiplication
Remember

A subspace must contain 0\mathbf 00 and be closed under addition and scalar multiplication; its dimension is the number of vectors in any of its bases.

Exam pattern: How this lecture has been examined
  • 2026 quizzes. Quiz 1 asked for the unit vector opposite to vvv and whether one feature was a linear combination of the others. Quiz 2 asked for a correlation, an inventory value c⊤qc^\top qc⊤q, the value of u⊤vu^\top vu⊤v from three norms, and sketches of the unit balls. Quiz 3 asked for the geometry of a span and a Gram–Schmidt computation.
  • Mid MCQs (2024, 2025). Characterisations of orthogonality; scaling, ∥kv∥=∣k∣ ∥v∥\|kv\|=|k|\,\|v\|∥kv∥=∣k∣∥v∥; norm properties; which vectors are unit vectors; definitions of independence and of span; subspace properties; properties of Gram–Schmidt; inner products of Boolean vectors; and "∥x∥=−∥−x∥\|x\|=-\|-x\|∥x∥=−∥−x∥ holds sometimes".
  • Mid problems. Gram–Schmidt on two or three vectors, including a dependent one; the order-dependence of Gram–Schmidt; the orthonormal membership test; inventory value and weight.
Remember: The one line for this lecture

Vectors are ordered lists; the inner product u⊤vu^\top vu⊤v yields length (u⊤u\sqrt{u^\top u}u⊤u​), angle, projection and orthogonality; and span, independence and basis say exactly which vectors a set can build — most conveniently through an orthonormal basis produced by Gram–Schmidt.
